content: Absinthe Wormwood, scientifically known as Artemisia absinthium (also referred to as Absinthe Wormwood, Wormwood, or Grand Wormwood), is a species of wormwood that is native to temperate regions of Europe, Asia, and northern Africa. It is a herbaceous perennial plant characterized by a hard, woody rhizome. The plant can grow up to 1.5 meters tall, with grooved, branched, and silvery-green stems. The leaves of the plant are arranged in a spiral pattern. They are greenish-grey on the upper surface and white on the underside, covered with silky, silvery-white hairs, and contain minute oil-producing glands. The basal leaves can grow up to 25 cm in length and are bipinnate to tripinnate with long petioles. The cauline leaves, which are located on the stem, are smaller (5–10 cm long), less divided, and have shorter petioles. The uppermost leaves may be simple and sessile, meaning they lack a petiole. The flowers of Absinthe Wormwood are pale yellow, tubular, and grouped in spherical, bent-down heads known as capitula. These capitula are further clustered into leafy and branched panicles. The plant flowers from early summer to early autumn, and pollination occurs via wind (anemophilous). The fruit is a small achene, and seed dispersal occurs through gravity. This plant naturally grows in uncultivated, arid areas, on rocky slopes, and along the edges of footpaths and fields. Cultivation and Uses Absinthe Wormwood can be easily cultivated in dry soil. It thrives in bright, sunny conditions and prefers fertile, nitrogen-rich soil. Propagation can be achieved through growth from ripened cuttings, which are typically taken in March or October in temperate climates, or by sowing seeds in nursery beds. The plant has been naturalized in areas outside its native range, including much of North America. The plant's distinctive odor makes it useful for creating a natural pest-repellent spray. In companion planting, the root secretions of Absinthe Wormwood inhibit the growth of surrounding plants, including weeds. It can repel insect larvae and is effective when planted at the edges of cultivated areas. Additionally, it has been used indoors to repel fleas and moths. Absinthe Wormwood is a key ingredient in the liquor absinthe and is also used to flavor other spirits and wines, such as vermouth and pelinkovac. Medicinally, it has been employed as a tonic, stomachic, febrifuge, and anthelmintic. Therapeutic Uses The leaves and flowering tops of the plant are harvested when it is in full bloom and are dried either naturally or with artificial heat. The active compounds in Absinthe Wormwood include silica, two bitter elements (absinthine and anabsinthine), thujone, tannic and resinous substances, malic acid, and succinic acid. Although thujone is a known hallucinogen, the plant has been traditionally used to alleviate indigestion and gastric pain, as well as for its antiseptic and febrifuge properties. For medicinal purposes, the herb is often prepared as a tea, which has been used to assist pregnant women during labor pain. A wine can also be made by macerating the herb. It is available in powder form and as a tincture. The oil extracted from the plant can act as a cardiac stimulant, improving blood circulation. However, pure wormwood oil is highly toxic and must be used with caution and in proper dosages to avoid harm. Wormwood is primarily recognized as a stomach medicine. The oil of Artemisia absinthium is a key ingredient in the topical liniment Absorbine Jr. Etymology and Folklore The term wormwood originates from Middle English wormwode or wermode. The modern form wormwood is influenced by its traditional use as a remedy for intestinal worms. An alternative etymological theory suggests that the word derives from Old English wermōd, which combines wer (meaning man, as in werewolf) and mōd (meaning mood). For further cultural and historical associations, including its connection to the Book of Revelation, Chernobyl, and other human cultural references, see the broader context of the genus Artemisia.
